+def _apply_replace_table(s, table):
+    """
+    Apply every replacement of a _replace_table to s in order. A replacement
+    is skipped when one of its two tokens cannot occur in s: present is a
+    superset of the code points of s (replacing only removes code points,
+    apart from the minted one, which is added whenever s changed), so the
+    skipped str.replace calls would not have changed s anyway.
+    """
+    present = set(s)
+    add = present.add
+    for ps, c, a, b in table:
+        if a in present and b in present:
+            n = len(s)
+            s = s.replace(ps, c)
+            if len(s) != n:
+                add(c)
+    return s

actions.reason: No accepted change. My one candidate skipped str.replace calls in the encode replacement table when a pair's tokens were missing from the string. It produced identical outputs, but it made both metrics worse: encode_ir ratio 1.0085, train_ir 1.0019. The per-merge Python check costs more than the C-level replace scans it saves. The library hot paths have already been optimised heavily. Fixed costs, like interpreter startup, importing and compiling the regex module, and corpus generation, seem to make up most of the ~370-410M instructions, but I have not measured that. I found no safe change that clears 1% within budget.

journal.text:
I tried to speed up encoding in minbpe by skipping str.replace calls in the encode replacement table whenever a pair's tokens were absent from the string. The edits touched minbpe/basic.py and minbpe/regex.py, 2 files and 36 lines per the guard.

My one sandbox evaluation was rejected for no improvement. Outputs were identical and both builds were fine, but encode_ir went from 408847232 to 412333863, ratio 1.0085 against a required 0.9900. train_ir went from 371496912 to 372203795, ratio 1.0019. I gave up without submitting a candidate.

I now believe a per-merge Python membership check costs more than the C-level replace scans it avoids. The hot paths in this code are already heavily optimised, so small Python-level guards inside the merge loop are a net loss.

Next time I should look for changes that cut the number of Python-level iterations rather than add checks inside them. One option is batching merges or reworking how the replacement table is built. I should also profile before editing.
